title: How Are We Saved?
subtitle: Grace, election, and the human will, with each serious view stated by its own best defenders
triageNote: This doctrine divides denominations, not the faith itself. A Calvinist and an Arminian who both trust Christ for salvation are brothers. They will worship in different buildings. They will sometimes argue late into the night. But they are saved by the same grace they disagree about describing.
question: When a person is saved, who does what? Does God choose us before we could choose anything, and then make us willing? Or does God offer grace to everyone and wait on a free human yes? When you came to faith, were you the one who reached? Or the one who had already been carried? The whole debate sits inside that single experience that almost every believer has had: looking back and not being sure whether you found God or God found you.
whyItMatters:
If you are new to faith, you may wonder why grown people who love the same Lord have fought over this for five hundred years. Here is the honest answer. How you understand salvation shapes how you pray, how you evangelize, how you handle the friend who walks away, and how you sleep at night when you doubt. If God chose you and holds you, your security rests entirely outside yourself. If your free response matters in a way that can be reversed, then your daily yes carries real weight. And real warning.

It shapes how you read your own story. The person who believes God did everything will fall to their knees in gratitude they did not earn. The person who believes they freely responded will feel the dignity of a love that was not forced. Both are trying to protect something precious. One protects the freeness of grace. The other protects the goodness of God and the reality of human choice. You cannot understand the people in your church until you understand what each side is afraid of losing.

positions.name: Calvinism (Reformed)
positions.inOneLine: Salvation is God's work from first to last. He chooses, He calls, He gives the faith by which we believe, and He keeps us to the end.
positions.bestCase:
Start with what you actually were before grace. The Bible does not say you were sick and needing help. It says you were dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1). A dead man does not cooperate with his own resurrection. He is raised. So when God saves, He does not wait at the door of a will that is free to refuse Him forever. He gives a new heart, and the new heart wants Him. This is what we mean by regeneration, the new birth, God making a dead person alive so that faith becomes possible at all. Regeneration comes first, and faith follows from it.

We hold to monergism, a word that simply means one worker. In the decisive moment of being made alive, God acts and we receive. We do not add the last crucial piece. If we did, then in the end the difference between the saved and the lost would be something in us, some better choice, some softer heart we produced on our own. And then heaven would have one small room for boasting. Grace that depends on my decision is grace I can take partial credit for. We refuse that.

Election, then, is God's choice before the foundation of the world to set His love on a people (Ephesians 1:4-5). It is not God looking down the corridor of time, seeing who would choose Him, and ratifying their choice. It is unconditional. He chose Jacob and not Esau before either had done anything good or bad, so that God's purpose of election would stand, not because of works but because of Him who calls (Romans 9:11). This is humbling, and it is meant to be.

And because salvation is His work, it cannot finally fail. Those whom He predestined He called, those He called He justified, those He justified He glorified (Romans 8:30). The chain does not break in the middle. This is perseverance, the certainty that the one who began a good work in you will complete it (Philippians 1:6). Your assurance does not rest on the strength of your grip on God. It rests on the strength of His grip on you.

We know the hard part. We know it sounds as if God could save everyone and chooses not to. We do not pretend that is easy. But we would rather sit with a hard truth that exalts God's freedom than soften it to fit what we find comfortable. Paul anticipated your objection. He did not resolve it. He asked, who are you, O man, to answer back to God (Romans 9:20). We let that question stand.

positions.name: Arminianism (Wesleyan)
positions.inOneLine: God's grace goes first and makes a free response possible, but that grace can be received or resisted, because love that cannot be refused is not love.
positions.bestCase:
Let us clear away the worst caricature right at the start. We do not believe you save yourself. We believe you were dead in sin and could not take one step toward God on your own. Every Arminian worth reading affirms total depravity as strongly as any Calvinist. The whole question is what God does about that deadness.

Our answer is prevenient grace, grace that comes before. The word prevenient just means going ahead of you. Before you ever sought God, God was already at work in you, drawing, awakening, freeing the will that sin had bound, so that for the first time you were able to say yes or no. This is not you producing faith out of your own goodness. It is God restoring enough freedom that a real response becomes possible. The grace is entirely a gift. The response is genuinely yours.

Why do we insist the response can be refused? Because Scripture is full of grief over people who would not come. Jesus wept, how often I wanted to gather your children, and you were not willing (Matthew 23:37). Stephen told the council, you always resist the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:51). If grace cannot be resisted, these tears and these rebukes lose their meaning. We take God at His word when He says He desires all to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). We cannot believe He secretly desires the opposite for most of them.

This is synergism, a word meaning working together. Not equal partners, never that. God provides the grace, the power, the initiative, the whole of salvation. We contribute nothing but the empty hands of faith that receive it. But the receiving is real, and it is ours, and it could have been withheld. Election, on our view, is God's choice to save those who are in Christ by faith. He foreknew His people. He set His love on them. And that love is wide enough to have included anyone who would come.

Why do we hold this? We are protecting the character of God. We cannot worship a God who creates persons specifically to pass them by when saving them would have cost Him nothing more than He already paid. The cross was for the world (John 3:16, 1 John 2:2). We would rather carry the mystery of why some refuse a real offer than the mystery of a love that was never actually offered to most.

positions.name: Provisionism (Traditionalist / Southern Baptist)
positions.inOneLine: God has provided salvation for everyone in the cross, and the gospel itself, heard and believed, is the means by which the lost are made able to respond.
positions.bestCase:
We are sometimes lumped in with the Arminians, but we differ on something important. So hear us on our own terms. We do not build our view on prevenient grace as a separate work poured into every heart. We build it on the gospel itself. The word of God is living and active. And faith comes by hearing the message of Christ (Romans 10:17). When the good news is preached, it carries its own power to enable belief. You do not need a hidden prior operation in the soul. You need the cross preached and the Spirit using that preaching.

On the human condition, we take sin with full seriousness. People are lost, condemned, unable to save themselves. But we do not read the deadness of Ephesians 2 as an inability to respond to the gospel when God calls through it. We read the Bible's relentless commands to repent and believe as real commands to real people who, by the gospel, can actually obey. God does not mock the lost by commanding what they have no capacity to do.

On election, we hold that God's saving choice is corporate and conditional. He determined to save those in Christ. Whoever believes is chosen in Him. We do not find in Scripture the idea that God, before creation, selected specific individuals for heaven and left the rest with no genuine opportunity. We find a God whose provision is universal, whose call goes out to all, and who saves all who trust His Son.

This is the view written into our churches' confession when Southern Baptists drafted a statement on salvation in 2012. It tries to say plainly what ordinary believers have always assumed from the pulpit: Christ died for everyone, the offer is sincere to everyone, and no one perishes because God secretly withheld the ability to come.

We hold this because we want the invitation to be honest. When we stand and say whosoever will may come, we mean it without crossed fingers. We are not protecting human pride. We are protecting the plain sense of a thousand gospel pleadings. God is not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). We take that to mean exactly what it says.

biblicalEvidence.summary: You were dead in trespasses, and God made you alive together with Christ. Salvation is by grace through faith, and even that is not your own doing, it is the gift of God, so that no one may boast.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arminians agree we were dead and that grace is the gift. They argue the gift offered can still be received or declined, and that the faith spoken of as a gift is the gift made possible by prevenient grace, not an irresistible deposit. Provisionists read deadness as guilt and helplessness to self-rescue, not as inability to respond to the preached gospel.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Before the twins had done anything, God said the older will serve the younger, that His purpose of election might stand. He has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills. Who are you to answer back to God?
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arminians and Provisionists argue Paul is discussing God's choice of nations and roles in redemptive history, Israel and the nations, not the eternal destiny of individuals. Jacob and Esau stand for peoples. The mercy in view is God's freedom to set the terms of salvation, which He has set as faith in Christ open to all.

biblicalEvidence.summary: All that the Father gives me will come to me. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And those given to Jesus He will raise on the last day.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arminians point out the same chapter says the Father draws and then adds, in John 12:32, that Jesus lifted up will draw all people. They take the drawing as wide and resistible. Provisionists stress that the drawing happens through the Father's word and teaching, verse 45, everyone who has heard and learned comes, which they read as the gospel doing its work, not a selective inward pull.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children together, and you were not willing. Jesus expresses a real desire. It meets a real refusal.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Calvinists note the verse contrasts the children Jesus wanted to gather with the leaders who would not let Him, so the unwillingness may belong to the leaders blocking the people. They also distinguish God's revealed desire that all repent from His hidden decree, holding both without collapsing one into the other.

biblicalEvidence.summary: God our Savior desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. The Lord is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Calvinists argue all here means all kinds of people, kings and commoners, Jew and Gentile, not every individual without exception. In 2 Peter, they read the any and the all as the elect, those God is patiently gathering, so that none of His own will be lost before the end.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Those God foreknew He predestined, and those He predestined He called, justified, and glorified. The unbroken chain holds from eternity past to glory.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arminians read foreknew in its relational sense, God set His love beforehand on those He knew would be His in Christ, and the chain describes what is true of all who are in Christ by faith. They note glorified is stated of a group, a people, not a proof that no individual can fall away.

biblicalEvidence.summary: If you confess with your mouth and believe in your heart, you will be saved. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Calvinists fully affirm the call goes out to all and that faith comes by hearing. They add that the effectual call within the outward call is what makes some hearers believe, so the preaching is God's ordinary means, not a power that works the same in every heart that hears it.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Those once enlightened, who tasted the heavenly gift and shared in the Holy Spirit, if they fall away, cannot be restored to repentance. A sober warning that real participants can apostatize.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Calvinists read this as a hypothetical warning God uses as a means to keep His people persevering, or as describing those who tasted the things of God outwardly without ever being truly born again, as 1 John 2:19 says, they went out from us because they were not of us. The warning is real. And it is effective precisely because it produces the perseverance it commands.

biblicalEvidence.summary: When the Gentiles heard this they rejoiced, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. Belief follows divine appointment.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Provisionists and some Arminians argue the verb can carry the sense of those who had set themselves toward, or were disposed to, eternal life, or that the appointment is to the offer now extended to Gentiles in redemptive history. The point of the verse, they say, is the opening of salvation to the nations. Not a roster of predestined individuals.

weighing:
What follows is my own reading. It is offered as one pastor's judgment and not as a verdict the church has settled. Hold it loosely. People far holier and far smarter than I am have landed in each of these camps, and I have buried saints from all three.

When I sit with the whole of Scripture, the texts that exalt God's initiative seem to me to carry more weight than I once wanted them to. Ephesians 2, John 6, and Romans 8 keep pressing the same direction, that the dead do not raise themselves and that the love which saves was reaching for me before I knew to reach back. The instinct behind the Reformed view, that grace is so free it leaves no room for boasting, feels true to my own conversion, where the more honest I am the less I find any good decision of mine to credit.

And yet I cannot make the tears of Matthew 23 disappear. And I will not try. When Jesus grieves over the ones who would not come, He means it, and the Arminian and the Provisionist are guarding something I dare not lose, that God's invitations are sincere and His grief is honest and the lost are not stage props in a script that condemned them before they drew breath. The strongest Calvinists I trust hold the sincere offer and the free decree together and refuse to soften either, and that is where I try to stand, often badly.

So here is my tentative resting place. I lean toward God's grace going first and going deepest, toward the conviction that if I am saved at all it is because He carried me. But I refuse to use that conviction to flatten the mystery of why some refuse a real offer, and I refuse to speak of the lost as if their refusal were not truly theirs. The deepest knot, how God's sovereignty and human responsibility are both fully true, I will not pretend to untie. Paul did not untie it. He worshiped in front of it (Romans 11:33). I think that is the only honest place to end.
charitableDisagreement:
If you hold a different view than the one I lean toward, here is what I want you to hear from me. The thoughtful Arminian is not soft on grace and is not exalting human pride. He is defending the goodness of God against a picture he finds unbearable, and he reads the same Bible on his knees. The thoughtful Calvinist is not a fatalist who thinks evangelism is pointless. He preaches the gospel to everyone precisely because preaching is how God calls His own, and he weeps over the lost as hard as anyone. The thoughtful Provisionist is not dodging the hard texts. He is fighting to keep the gospel invitation honest at the altar. Each of them is protecting a real treasure, and each fears the other will lose it.

Is this a hill to die on? No. It is a hill to think hard on, to pray over, to argue about with people you love and then take communion beside. The line that divides the faith is not Calvin from Wesley. It is whether you trust Christ crucified and risen for your salvation at all. On that, all three of these views stand on the same side of the only chasm that finally matters. Do not let a second-order debate fool you into treating a brother as an enemy.

relatedDebates.note: For whom did Christ die? Calvinists who hold particular redemption say the cross actually secured salvation for the elect, otherwise Christ died for many who are never saved and the cross is a payment that does not pay. Arminians and Provisionists hold a general atonement, that Christ truly died for all (1 John 2:2, 1 Timothy 2:6), and that the cross provides salvation for everyone while applying it only to those who believe. Many Reformed Baptists take a middle path, sometimes called sufficient for all and efficient for the elect.

relatedDebates.topic: Perseverance versus the possibility of apostasy
relatedDebates.note: Can a truly saved person be finally lost? Calvinists say no, the elect will persevere because God preserves them (John 10:28-29, Philippians 1:6), and those who fall away show they were never truly regenerate (1 John 2:19). Classical Arminians and many Provisionists say a genuine believer can, through settled unbelief, fall away (Hebrews 6, Hebrews 10:26-29). Note that most Southern Baptists affirm eternal security even while rejecting unconditional election, so the camps do not line up as neatly as people assume.

relatedDebates.topic: Justification and the New Perspective on Paul
relatedDebates.note: Justification is God declaring a guilty person righteous in Christ. The Reformation taught it is by faith alone, apart from works, with Christ's righteousness credited to us. The New Perspective, associated with E.P. Sanders, James Dunn, and N.T. Wright, argues that Paul's fight against works of the law was less about earning salvation by good deeds and more about the badges of Jewish identity, circumcision and food laws, that wrongly excluded Gentiles. Critics like John Piper warn this can blur the credited righteousness of Christ that gives believers their security. Defenders reply that they are recovering Paul's actual first century setting, not denying grace. This one cuts across the Calvinist and Arminian divide entirely.
